raw:
**Move note.** Opening thoughts on the shape of this game. The center-occupation win is the realistic target: my team needs all four of (3,3), (3,4), (4,3), (4,4) at once. Turn order gives Team A the first move of each round, but Blue can reach the right-hand center squares in one move and Green the left-hand ones, so a pure race just ends 2–2. The game will be decided by captures around the center.

The critical structural fact is that my two colors cannot sandwich as a pair — a Red piece and a Yellow piece flanking an enemy do nothing. So each color has to build its own flanking pairs. That suggests a natural division of labour: **Red owns row 3, Yellow owns row 4.** Red starts on the top edge and can drop straight down any empty column onto row 3; Yellow does the same upward onto row 4. Any enemy piece that lands on row 3 with a Red already beside it and an empty row-3 square on its far side is dead the moment I drop another Red down that column. That makes the two rows containing the centre squares genuinely hostile territory for Blue and Green, rather than just a race.

So I start by claiming a centre square with Red and beginning the row-3 occupation: (0,3) down to (3,3). The column is clear, the destination is empty, and it lands on a centre square. It also sets up the punishment pattern immediately — if Green comes along row 3 to (3,2) to crowd me, Red answers (0,1)–(3,1) and the sandwich (3,1)R–(3,2)G–(3,3)R takes it; if Blue drops into (3,4), Red answers (0,5)–(3,5) and takes that instead. Either way, contesting row 3 costs the opponent material.

The thing I have to keep watching is the mirror-image danger: a column sandwich by one enemy colour spanning both a Red on row 3 and a Yellow on row 4 would capture *both* my pieces at once, since a sandwich line may mix colours and my teammate's pieces are not immune. So as I fill row 3 and row 4 I need to make sure the squares at (2,c) and (5,c) aren't both available to the same enemy colour. I'll keep the column-2/column-5 approach squares in mind every turn.

Plan for the next few moves: Yellow takes (4,3) or (4,4), Red adds a second row-3 piece, and I look to punish the first enemy piece that commits to row 3 or row 4.

raw:
**Move note.** Blue has planted a piece on the centre square (4,4), and I want to make that commitment expensive rather than just racing it.

Yellow can't sandwich together with Red — teammate colours don't pair — so Yellow has to build its own flanking pair, and row 4 is exactly where Yellow can do that, dropping straight up any empty column from the bottom edge. I'm playing (7,5) up to (4,5), sitting right beside the Blue centre piece. The threat is immediate: next Yellow turn, (7,3) runs up column 3 to (4,3), and the Blue piece at (4,4) is caught between two Yellows and dies. That follow-up move also happens to land on a centre square, so the capture and the centre claim are the same move.

The reason I prefer this to grabbing (4,3) right now is a trap that Blue and Green can easily walk into. If either of them blocks (4,3) to stop the sandwich, they don't defuse it — they extend it. A sandwich line may contain several pieces of mixed colours as long as both ends are mine, so with (4,3) enemy-occupied and (4,4) Blue, Yellow simply runs (7,2) up to (4,2) and takes *both* pieces at once. Column 2 is clear all the way. Green's only route into the centre is along row 4 to (4,3), since row 3 is blocked by my Red at (3,3) and Green has nothing in column 4 — so the one centre square Green can reach is the one that costs it a piece.

I'm also deliberately avoiding stacking Red on (3,3) with Yellow on (4,3). That column pair is the shape I warned myself about: Green plays (2,0)–(2,3) and later (5,0)–(5,3), and a single sandwich swallows the Red *and* the Yellow together, because my teammate's pieces are not immune to being inside an enemy line. Keeping Yellow off (4,3) for now means Green's column-3 idea can only ever win one piece, and Red can dodge sideways to (3,4) — still a centre square — if it gets serious.

Meanwhile (3,4) is poisoned for Blue: if Blue drops in there, Red answers (0,5) down to (3,5) and the piece is sandwiched against my Red on (3,3).

raw:
**Move note.** Green has walked straight into the row-4 trap: the centre row now reads (4,3) Green, (4,4) Blue, (4,5) Yellow. A sandwich line may hold several pieces of mixed colours as long as both ends are my moving colour, so Yellow running (7,2) up an empty column 2 to (4,2) would take the Green *and* the Blue in one stroke. That threat is live for my next Yellow turn, and Blue's only defences are to block column 2 from the right along row 5 or 6, or to run the (4,4) piece away — I can't stop either, so I'll spend this Red move on the other side of the board.

Because the more urgent thing is that Green's centre piece cuts both ways. With Green sitting on (4,3), my Red on (3,3) is one move from death: Green plays (2,0) along the empty row 2 to (2,3), and my Red is caught vertically between (2,3) and (4,3). Green's turn comes at ply 7, after my Yellow move, so if Blue does block column 2 I would have no way to answer in time — Red doesn't move again until ply 8, one turn too late.

So I'm slamming the door now: (0,2) drops down to (2,2), planting a Red in the middle of row 2. Green's row-2 piece at (2,0) can no longer slide to (2,3), and there's no other Green route to that square — column 3 has no Green above, and the horizontal flank pair (3,2)+(3,4) is impossible for Green because row 3 is blocked by my own Red and Green has nothing in column 4. Red on (3,3) becomes hard to attack.

The new piece is also useful rather than purely defensive. If Green tries the vertical answer (3,0)–(3,2), I take it with (0,1) down to (3,1), sandwiching it against my Red on (3,3). If Green tries (1,0)–(1,2) instead, I take it by sliding (0,1) sideways to (0,2) and squeezing it against the new Red on (2,2).

One principle I want to hold onto: pre-placing *both* flanking squares is worthless, since captures only fire on my own move. The value is in holding one flank and keeping the other reachable — that's what makes (3,4) poisoned for Blue and row 4 poisoned for Green.

raw:
**Move note.** The trap closes. Yellow runs (7,2) straight up the empty column 2 to (4,2), and row 4 now reads Yellow–Green–Blue–Yellow: an unbroken line of non-Yellow pieces at (4,3) and (4,4) with my own Yellow waiting at (4,5) on the far side. Both of them come off the board in a single move — Green's centre piece and Blue's centre piece together. That's one loss charged to each of them, a third of the way to eliminating both colours, and it clears two of the four centre squares at once.

Blue spent its turn on (3,7)–(3,4) rather than blocking column 2, which was the one defence available — a piece dropped on (5,2) or (6,2) from the right would have cut Yellow's path and forced me to find something else. Instead Blue reinforced the centre, and that reinforcement is about to be stranded.

More to the point, Blue's new piece on (3,4) is landing in the square I already flagged as poisoned. After this capture it sits directly beside my Red on (3,3) with (3,5) empty and column 5 wide open, so my next Red turn is (0,5) down to (3,5) and the Blue piece is sandwiched. Red moves at ply 8, before Blue moves again at ply 9, so Blue cannot save it itself — only Green, moving in between, can interfere, and its one way to do so is (1,0) sliding along row 1 to (1,5) to plug the column. Row 2 is unavailable to Green because my Red on (2,2) blocks it, which is exactly the job I gave that piece.

After this move my remaining exposure is Yellow on (4,5): Blue can attack it by pairing (3,5) with (5,5), or by dropping back into (4,4) and reaching (4,6). Both take two Blue moves and I get turns in between, so I can dodge or counter. I'll keep watching that the same enemy colour never gets both flanking squares of one of my pieces.

raw:
**Move note.** Blue's piece on (3,4) is caught, and taking it is worth more than the other capture on offer.

I have two captures available this turn. Red (0,1) down to (3,1) would sandwich Green's new piece on (3,2) against my Red on (3,3); Red (0,5) down to (3,5) sandwiches Blue's (3,4) against the same Red. The tiebreaker is who moves next. Blue acts immediately after me, so the (3,4) piece walks away if I don't take it now. Green doesn't act until ply 11, and its piece on (3,2) has almost nowhere to run — column 2 is sealed above by my Red on (2,2) and below by my Yellow on (4,2), so it can only shuffle to (3,1) or (3,0) along row 3. That capture will keep.

Green does have a counter: (1,0) along row 1 to (1,2) would take my Red on (2,2), squeezing it against (3,2). I'm accepting that trade, because if it happens I answer with (0,1)–(3,1) and take the Green piece anyway, leaving both enemy colours on two losses — one capture from elimination each, at which point their surviving pieces turn to Void and can never capture again.

Checking my own move for friendly fire, since a sandwich line swallows teammate pieces too: looking down from (3,5) I see my Yellow on (4,5), but the square beyond it, (5,5), is empty, so that line breaks harmlessly. Only the Blue on (3,4) comes off.

The bigger picture is that this clears the last enemy piece out of the four central squares, and neither opponent can put one back quickly. Blue has nothing left in row 3, row 4, or column 3/4 — its remaining pieces are all on column 7 — so it cannot reach a centre square in a single move. Green is worse off: row 4 is blocked by my Yellow on (4,2), row 3 by my own Red, and it has nothing in columns 3 or 4.

So the plan is concrete: Yellow takes (4,4) up the clear column 4, Red fills (3,4) from (0,4), and Yellow completes with (4,3) — reachable either sideways from (4,2) or straight up column 3. Four centre squares, four of my pieces, and the game ends there.

raw:
**Move note.** Blue has shifted (2,7) to (2,5), presumably heading for (2,4) and then down into the empty centre square (3,4). I intend to be there first, and this move starts the finishing sequence.

Yellow slides one square from (4,2) to (4,3). Two things at once. It claims a second centre square, and it steps out of a real threat: Green's piece on (3,2) meant that (5,0) running along row 5 to (5,2) would have caught my Yellow on (4,2) between two Greens. That piece was going to be attacked next turn; now it's on a square that matters instead.

I checked the move for friendly fire before committing, since a sandwich line takes teammate pieces too. Looking up from (4,3) I see my own Red on (3,3), but the square beyond it, (2,3), is empty, so the line breaks and nothing of mine is touched. The enclosure check is also clean — the Red/Green group around (3,2) still has empty squares beside it.

What makes this decisive is that the two remaining centre squares, (3,4) and (4,4), are now unreachable for both opponents. Row 4 is sealed at both ends by my Yellows on (4,3) and (4,5); Green has nothing in column 4 and row 3 is blocked for it by my Red on (3,3); Blue's remaining pieces sit on (2,5), (1,7), (5,7), (6,7), none of which can reach a centre square in a single move. Green moves next and cannot take either square; Blue moves at ply 13 and cannot either.

So the finish is: Red takes (3,4) on my next turn — from (0,4) straight down the clear column, or, if Green plugs column 4 by running (1,0) along row 1 to (1,4), simply (3,5) sideways one square, which nothing can block. Then Yellow completes the set on (4,4), again with an unblockable one-square move from (4,5) if the column route is cut. Four centre squares, all Team A, and the game ends on ply 14.

The only thing my opponents can profitably do in the meantime is take my Red on (2,2) with Green's (1,0)–(1,2). That piece has done its job and isn't part of the finish.

raw:
**Move note.** Red drops from (0,4) straight down the empty column 4 to (3,4), taking the third of the four central squares. The centre now reads Red on (3,3), Red on (3,4), Yellow on (4,3) — only (4,4) is left.

I chose the piece from the back rank rather than sliding my Red on (3,5) sideways, because (3,5) is doing useful work: it plugs column 5 and keeps Blue's piece on (2,5) from dropping down that file. No reason to give that up when the top-rank Red has a clear run.

The move itself is quiet — every direction out of (3,4) either runs into my own Red or into an empty square, so there's no capture and, more importantly, no accidental friendly fire on my own men.

Now the position is closed for both opponents. Blue's four remaining pieces sit on (1,7), (2,5), (5,7) and (6,7). None of them can reach (4,4) in a single move: column 4 is empty of Blue, row 4 from the right is sealed by my Yellow on (4,5), and (2,5) can't come down column 5 because my Red on (3,5) is in the way. Blue also has no way to capture any of my three centre pieces — every sandwich would need two Blue pieces placed on specific squares, and Blue can only play one move. Green doesn't act again until ply 15, which is after this is over.

So Yellow finishes next turn with (4,5) to (4,4). That's a one-square step to an adjacent square, which means it cannot be blocked by anything short of occupying (4,4) itself — and I've just established that neither opponent can do that. Even if Blue plants a piece on (5,4) to cut the column-4 route from my back rank, the sideways move still works.

Four central squares held by Red and Yellow together wins immediately under the centre-occupation rule, and mixing my two colours is explicitly allowed. Barring something I've miscounted, the game ends on ply 14.

note:
**Move note.** Red drops from (0,4) straight down the empty column 4 to (3,4), taking the third of the four central squares. The centre now reads Red on (3,3), Red on (3,4), Yellow on (4,3) — only (4,4) is left.

I chose the piece from the back rank rather than sliding my Red on (3,5) sideways, because (3,5) is doing useful work: it plugs column 5 and keeps Blue's piece on (2,5) from dropping down that file. No reason to give that up when the top-rank Red has a clear run.

The move itself is quiet — every direction out of (3,4) either runs into my own Red or into an empty square, so there's no capture and, more importantly, no accidental friendly fire on my own men.

Now the position is closed for both opponents. Blue's four remaining pieces sit on (1,7), (2,5), (5,7) and (6,7). None of them can reach (4,4) in a single move: column 4 is empty of Blue, row 4 from the right is sealed by my Yellow on (4,5), and (2,5) can't come down column 5 because my Red on (3,5) is in the way. Blue also has no way to capture any of my three centre pieces — every sandwich would need two Blue pieces placed on specific squares, and Blue can only play one move. Green doesn't act again until ply 15, which is after this is over.

So Yellow finishes next turn with (4,5) to (4,4). That's a one-square step to an adjacent square, which means it cannot be blocked by anything short of occupying (4,4) itself — and I've just established that neither opponent can do that. Even if Blue plants a piece on (5,4) to cut the column-4 route from my back rank, the sideways move still works.

Four central squares held by Red and Yellow together wins immediately under the centre-occupation rule, and mixing my two colours is explicitly allowed. Barring something I've miscounted, the game ends on ply 14.

raw:
**Move note.** Blue found the shot I missed: (5,7) along row 5 to (5,5) caught my Yellow on (4,5) and my Red on (3,5) in one vertical line, with its piece on (2,5) as the far anchor. That's the exact pattern I'd been warning myself about — a single enemy sandwich swallowing a Red and a Yellow together, since teammate pieces are not immune inside the line. I had checked (2,5) as an attacker but not as an anchor for a piece arriving from below.

It doesn't matter, because it didn't touch the centre. Three of the four central squares are still mine — Red on (3,3), Red on (3,4), Yellow on (4,3) — and (4,4) is empty. Blue spent its turn taking material on column 5 instead of occupying that square, and it's Yellow to move.

Column 4 is completely clear from my back rank: (6,4), (5,4) and (4,4) are all empty, so Yellow runs (7,4) straight up to (4,4).

Before playing it I checked the move can't undo itself. Looking up from (4,4) I see my own Red on (3,4), but the square beyond it at (2,4) is empty, so that line breaks and no friendly piece is taken. To the left is my own Yellow, which a sandwich can't act on at all. The Red group on (3,3)–(3,4) still has empty squares beside it, so there's no enclosure either. The move is clean.

That puts Red, Red, Yellow, Yellow on (3,3), (3,4), (4,3) and (4,4) — all four central squares held by Team A. The centre-occupation rule explicitly allows any mix of a team's colours, and it wins the instant the condition holds.
